Aerospace Composite NDT 2026: PAUT vs Thermography vs UT

Comprehensive guide to Aerospace Composite Inspection. Explore principles, standards, and best practices for effective implementation.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · March 2026 · Industry-Specific

Industry Overview

The aerospace industry relies on advanced composite materials for 50% of new aircraft structures, with next-generation narrow-body aircraft like Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 featuring 80%+ composite construction by weight. Carbon fiber reinforced polymers (CFRP), glass fiber composites (GRP), aramid fiber composites, and advanced hybrid materials represent the future of aircraft design, enabling lighter weight, improved fuel efficiency (15-20% fuel savings), and enhanced performance characteristics. These materials offer exceptional strength-to-weight ratios (up to 5 times higher than aluminum) but introduce unique inspection challenges absent in traditional aluminum structures. Composite damage modes including delamination, fiber breakage, matrix cracking, and moisture absorption develop differently than metal fatigue and corrosion, requiring specialized NDT methods and inspector training. FAA AC 20-107B and EASA Special Conditions requirements mandate comprehensive composite inspection programs ensuring aircraft safety with the same rigor applied to aluminum structures. NDT plays a critical role enabling aircraft manufacturers and operators to detect composite damage before it compromises structural integrity, with inspection costs representing 2-4% of manufacturing and maintenance budgets but preventing failures costing billions in liability and lost aircraft.

Common Defects and Failure Modes

Aerospace composite structures experience specific damage mechanisms requiring targeted NDT detection methods and specialized repair approaches. Delamination, the most common composite defect (40-50% of damage discoveries), occurs when layers separate internally from impact damage, manufacturing defects, environmental exposure, or cyclic loading. Matrix cracking develops from overstress, moisture absorption causing swelling and internal stress, or thermal cycling creating differential expansion. Fiber breakage from impact, bearing stress concentration at fasteners, or overload reduces load-carrying capacity proportional to the number of broken fibers. Porosity and void content from manufacturing defects including trapped air, incomplete wetting, and volatile outgassing weaken composite strength, particularly affecting matrix-dominated properties like shear strength and transverse compression. Water absorption causes epoxy matrix swelling (1-3% by volume), reducing glass transition temperature, lowering modulus and strength, particularly at elevated temperatures, and creating internal stress concentration sites. Microcracking in resin-rich areas develops from manufacturing defects or service stress, creating pathways for moisture ingress and crack propagation. Disbond at fastener holes develops from stress concentration or inadequate surface preparation before bonding. Wrinkles and waviness in fiber alignment from manufacturing errors create local stress concentrations that initiate crack growth under cyclic loading.

NDT Methods Used

Aerospace composite inspection employs multiple complementary NDT techniques optimized for composite material properties and defect detection sensitivity. Ultrasonic testing (UT) per ASTM E2375 and MIL-HDBK-1823 detects internal defects including delamination, porosity, and fiber waviness using pulse-echo, immersion, and through-transmission modes with frequencies 5-25 MHz. Phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) enables rapid full-area scanning with superior sensitivity to delamination extent, providing 3D characterization without physical probe manipulation. Thermography per ASTM E591 detects subsurface delaminations and voids through temperature differential patterns under active heating or thermal excitation with 0.05°C sensitivity. Flash thermography (pulsed thermography) provides rapid large-area coverage for quality assurance inspections on large composite panels. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables non-contact imaging of near-surface layers (1-2mm depth) without contact pressure, valuable for delicate composite structures and painted surfaces. Terahertz imaging detects moisture content and structural features through composite thickness. X-ray and computed tomography (CT) provide detailed volumetric defect characterization for failure investigation and precise defect sizing. Shearography detects stress-induced deformation patterns revealing hidden defects through non-contact measurement. Eddy current testing on conductive composites detects fiber breakage and matrix cracking near conductive surfaces.

Inspection Procedures and Intervals

FAA AC 20-107B and EASA Special Conditions establish composite inspection program requirements integrated into aircraft structural maintenance planning and continuing airworthiness monitoring. In-service composite inspection starts with visual/optical inspection per FAA AC 20-107B Appendix A, identifying external damage, delamination shadows, moisture staining, disbond indicators, and exposed fibers requiring detailed investigation. Tap testing per Boeing D6-54445 enables technicians to detect delaminations through audible tone changes. UT baseline inspections establish defect-free reference signatures for damage trending. FAA requires large transport aircraft to undergo comprehensive composite visual inspection every 2,000 flight hours or 18 months, whichever occurs first, with more frequent inspections for high-risk pressure vessel areas. Flight damage discovery triggers immediate UT investigation and quantitative defect characterization using ASTM E2375 procedures. Maintenance inspections following structural repairs mandate UT verification that repairs achieved required strength per repair design specification. Pressurized fuselage areas receive heightened inspection frequency (1,000 FH intervals) due to cyclic loading and moisture ingress risk. Bonded structure inspections focus on adhesive failure modes at wing-fuselage, tail, and control surface attachments. High-vibration areas including engine nacelle pylons and control surface hinges receive enhanced monitoring for crack initiation and fatigue damage.

Equipment and Technology

Aerospace composite NDT requires specialized equipment meeting stringent quality standards and AS9100 traceability requirements. Portable ultrasonic thickness/flaw detectors specifically suitable for composite inspection (a significant capital item) must accommodate low acoustic impedance (Z=1.5-2.5 MRayl) and high attenuation, with A-scan/B-scan displays. Automated UT scanning systems (a significant capital item) provide consistent full-area coverage with data mapping and defect sizing for fleet documentation. Thermal imaging cameras with temperature measurement accuracy and data logging (a significant capital item) detect delamination through surface temperature patterns under active or passive heating. Flash thermography systems (a significant capital item) enable rapid full-component thermal scanning covering large areas (0.5-2 m²) in seconds. Portable optical coherence tomography (OCT) systems (a significant capital item) provide near-surface defect imaging without contact pressure, valuable for thin composite details. X-ray and CT systems (a significant capital item) provide detailed defect characterization for failure investigation and support design validation. Shearography systems (a significant capital item) enable stress-induced deformation imaging with electronic speckle pattern interferometry (ESPI). Data acquisition software (a significant capital item) manages inspection scheduling, results documentation, defect database, and trending analysis. Complete inspection equipment packages for aircraft manufacturers cost varies with capability with ongoing calibration and maintenance.

Certification Requirements

FAA and EASA require aerospace composite inspectors to demonstrate extensive composite materials knowledge, damage mechanisms understanding, and hands-on inspection experience. Formal composite structure NDT certification programs (120-160 hours) cover composite materials science, laminate theory, damage mechanisms, NDT method theory and application, defect interpretation using ASTM E2375 criteria, and repair design criteria per FAA AC 20-107B. Certification requires documented training completion and written examination demonstrating comprehensive knowledge of composites, defects, and NDT methods. AS9100 quality system requirements mandate inspector qualification documentation and continuing education (typically 8 hours annually). Method-specific certifications include ASNT Level II certification for UT inspectors and PAUT specialists. Company-specific training on aircraft type-specific composite structure, inspection procedures, acceptance criteria, and repair limitations is mandatory before personnel perform production or in-service inspections. FAA Designated Inspection Representative (DIR) status requires extensive experience (10+ years), written examination, and continuing education, enabling inspectors to approve composite repairs. Recurrent training requirements ensure inspectors maintain current knowledge of evolving composite materials, manufacturing processes, and inspection techniques. Many aerospace companies require annual composite refresher training and periodic requalification assessments including practical inspection demonstrations.

Cost and ROI Analysis

Aerospace composite inspection represents a substantial investment in aircraft quality assurance, safety, and long-term reliability. Development and validation of composite inspection procedures for a new aircraft type costs a modest cost2,000,000 including procedure development, equipment qualification, and initial NDT survey establishment. In-service composite UT inspection costs a modest cost5,000 per aircraft per 2,000-flight-hour inspection cycle. Thermal imaging surveys for fleet damage screening and moisture detection cost varies with capability per aircraft. Damage investigations utilizing advanced imaging including CT or shearography cost varies with capability per incident. Annual fleet-wide composite inspection programs for major carriers (500+ aircraft) cost varies with capability million. Preventive composite inspection prevents catastrophic structural failures. Composite damage undetected until in-flight structural failure results in loss of life (300+ fatalities possible for large transport aircraft), catastrophic litigation exceeding a modest cost billion, fleet groundings preventing revenue generation, and irreparable damage to aircraft manufacturer reputation. Detected damage caught in advance is repairable: minor delamination repairs cost varies with capability; significant damage repairs cost varies with capability; detected damage prevents failures costing billions in liability. Airlines and manufacturers recognize that comprehensive composite inspection programs maintain fleet safety and reliability while reducing unscheduled maintenance surprises disrupting operations and generating customer dissatisfaction.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why are composites harder to inspect than aluminum? Composites have higher acoustic attenuation (10-50 dB/cm vs. 0.5 dB/cm for aluminum) and lower acoustic impedance (1.5-2.5 MRayl vs. 40 MRayl for aluminum), reducing UT penetration depth to 3-10 cm vs. 100+ cm. Composites are anisotropic with direction-dependent properties requiring angle-dependent inspection. Internal delaminations don't produce surface cracks like metal fatigue, requiring volumetric inspection methods.

2. What is delamination and how dangerous is it? Delamination is separation between composite plies or layers reducing through-thickness strength by 50-90%. Delaminations enable moisture ingress, progressively degrading matrix-dominated properties. Small delaminations spread under flight loads, eventually leading to catastrophic loss of load-carrying capability. Delamination detection is highest NDT priority in composite inspection.

3. Can tap testing detect all delamination? Tap testing detects moderate-to-large delaminations (area >2 cm²) but misses small defects, disbonds at fasteners, and internal damage in thick sections (>3mm). Tap testing is operator-dependent and subjective, with 15-40% miss rate depending on operator training. Ultrasonic testing provides objective, quantitative detection superior to tap testing for critical applications.

4. How does moisture affect composites? Moisture absorption lowers glass transition temperature (Tg) by 5-20°C, reducing composite strength and stiffness by 5-50% at service temperatures. Absorbed water causes matrix swelling and residual stress concentration. Moisture creates pathways for crack propagation and enables moisture-driven cracking under combined stress/moisture exposure. High-altitude humidity exposure in pressurized fuselages creates chronic moisture ingress requiring periodic drying and inspection.

5. Why is visual inspection insufficient for composite damage detection? Delaminations and internal damage don't produce visible surface cracks. Subsurface damage including matrix cracking and fiber breakage is invisible to visual inspection without painted-surface damage. Visual inspection catches only external damage including impact marks, scratches, and exposed fibers, missing 50-70% of dangerous internal defects.

6. What is difference between UT and thermography for composite inspection? UT provides precise depth measurement and defect sizing (±0.5mm) with sensitivity to small defects (0.5mm²); thermography detects delamination through thermal diffusivity changes but provides limited depth information (±2-3mm) and sensitivity limited to larger defects (>1 cm²). UT excels at detecting small defects; thermography enables rapid large-area screening. Optimal inspection combines both methods.

7. How often must aircraft composite structures be inspected? FAA AC 20-107B requires visual inspection every 2,000 flight hours or 18 months for transport aircraft. Advanced UT and thermography inspections occur every 4,000-8,000 flight hours during scheduled maintenance checks. Damage discovery triggers immediate detailed investigation per FAA AC 20-107B procedures.

8. Can repaired composite sections achieve original strength? Properly designed and executed composite repairs achieve 80-95% of original strength depending on damage size, location, repair design, and acceptance testing. Repair design depends on damage size, location relative to high-stress areas, and loading environment. Repairs include mechanical fastening, adhesive bonding, and composite patching per FAA-approved repair schemes. NDT verification ensures repairs achieved required strength through residual defect assessment.

9. What emerging composite inspection technologies are on the horizon? Permanently installed ultrasonic sensors enable continuous structural health monitoring and real-time damage detection. Artificial intelligence-assisted defect detection and characterization reducing subjective interpretation. Terahertz imaging provides enhanced defect contrast and moisture detection through composite thickness. Drone-based thermography enables rapid full-airframe inspection without scaffolding. Advanced composite materials including thermoplastics and nanocomposites will require new NDT approaches.

10. How do manufacturing defects affect composite inspection? Manufacturing voids, fiber waviness, resin-rich areas, ply waviness, dry fiber spots, and void clusters create weak points initiating damage under flight loads with 2-5 times lower fatigue life vs. ideal composites. In-process NDT during manufacturing detects defects enabling correction before parts enter service. In-service inspection monitors for crack initiation at manufacturing defect sites through trending of repeated inspections.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Aerospace composite inspection ensures safety and reliability of advanced aircraft structures while enabling the performance benefits of composite construction and improved fuel efficiency. Comprehensive NDT programs combining visual inspection, ultrasonic testing, thermography, and advanced imaging methods provide the confidence necessary for safe composite aircraft operation worldwide. Organizations investing in advanced composite inspection technologies, rigorous inspector training, and continuous procedure improvement maintain leadership in aerospace safety and quality.
